topic: Memory management: heap, bitmaps & trim memory

questions.question: What does `ActivityManager.getMemoryClass()` tell you?
options: The size of the shared zygote heap inherited by every app
The approximate Java/ART heap limit in MB for a normal app on this device
How much free RAM the device has right now
The native heap budget your process may use before being killed
questions.explanation: `getMemoryClass()` returns the per-app managed heap limit in megabytes, which you can use to size caches. It is a fixed device property, not a live free-RAM reading, and it says nothing about native allocations, which are not capped by this limit.

questions.question: Setting `android:largeHeap="true"` guarantees your app a bigger heap on every device, so it is a reliable fix for OutOfMemoryError.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: On some devices the large memory class is the same as the normal one, so the flag gives no extra room. Even where it helps, a bigger heap means longer GC work and more pressure on other apps; the right fix is to reduce what you hold, especially decoded bitmaps.

questions.question: Roughly how much memory does a decoded 1080 x 1920 bitmap take in `ARGB_8888`?
options: About 2 MB, the size of the JPEG file
About 4 MB
About 6 MB
About 8 MB
questions.explanation: `ARGB_8888` uses 4 bytes per pixel, so 1080 x 1920 x 4 is about 8.3 million bytes, roughly 8 MB. The compressed file size is irrelevant once decoded; about 4 MB would be `RGB_565` (2 bytes per pixel).

questions.question: Since Android 8.0, where do a software `Bitmap`'s pixels live, and what frees them?
options: In an ashmem region owned by SurfaceFlinger, freed when the app goes to background
In native memory, freed when the Bitmap object is collected or `recycle()` is called
In GPU memory only, freed when the window that drew it is destroyed
In a Java byte array on the managed heap, freed when the array is collected
questions.explanation: From Android 8.0 the pixel data is allocated in native memory and tied to the Java `Bitmap` object, so it is released when that object is garbage-collected (or earlier via `recycle()`). This is why a heap dump of the Java heap can look small while the process's native memory is large. GPU-only storage is the special case of `HARDWARE` bitmaps.

questions.question: Your image library decodes to `Bitmap.Config.HARDWARE`. Which code is most likely to break?
options: Animating the alpha of the `ImageView` that shows it
Showing the bitmap in an `ImageView` inside a RecyclerView
Running `Palette` on it or drawing it onto a software `Canvas`
Scaling it with `ImageView.ScaleType.CENTER_CROP`
questions.explanation: Hardware bitmaps keep their pixels only in graphics memory and are immutable, so CPU pixel access such as `getPixel()`/`Palette` and drawing into a software canvas fail. Displaying, scaling and animating them through the hardware-accelerated pipeline is exactly what they are designed for.

questions.question: Which of these actually reduce the memory a decoded image occupies? Select all that apply.
options: Storing the image as PNG on disk instead of JPEG
Calling `System.gc()` right after each decode
Asking the decoder for the target view size (e.g. `ImageDecoder.setTargetSize`)
Decoding with `inSampleSize` so a 4000 px photo comes in at a fraction of its size
Using `RGB_565` for opaque images where slight banding is acceptable
questions.explanation: Decoded size is width x height x bytes per pixel, so downsampling, decoding to the target size and a smaller pixel format all shrink it. The on-disk format only changes the compressed file, not the decoded pixels, and forcing GC does not shrink a bitmap you still reference.

questions.question: The user leaves your app; its process becomes cached. Later the device runs low on memory. What should your design assume?
options: The process is frozen but never killed while it still holds a reference to a ViewModel
The process may be killed outright with no further callbacks, so state must already be saved by `onStop()`
Cached processes are only killed after all foreground services on the device are stopped
The system calls `onDestroy()` on each activity before killing the process, so save state there
questions.explanation: The low memory killer picks processes by their importance (cached ones go first) and kills them with a signal, so no lifecycle callback is guaranteed after `onStop()`. That is why state belongs in `onSaveInstanceState`/SavedStateHandle and persistent storage, not in `onDestroy()`.

questions.question: `TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN` is delivered when all of your app's UI is no longer visible, which makes it a good point to release resources used only by the UI.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: This level fires when the user leaves your UI, unlike `onStop()` which fires for every activity transition inside your app. Releasing UI-only caches here makes your process cheaper to keep cached, so it is less likely to be killed and cold-started later.

questions.question: `dumpsys meminfo` shows your app's total PSS climbing, but the Java heap dump barely changes. Which categories could explain the growth? Select all that apply.
options: Graphics: GPU textures and buffers, including hardware bitmaps
Objects reachable from a static field in your Kotlin code
Native: e.g. bitmap pixels, native libraries, JNI allocations
Interned strings created by your JSON parser
questions.explanation: Native and Graphics memory are not part of the Java heap, so a Java heap dump will not show them even though they count toward the process's PSS. Objects held by static fields and interned strings are managed-heap objects and would appear in the heap dump.

questions.question: On modern Android, what must be true for `BitmapFactory.Options.inBitmap` to reuse an existing bitmap?
options: The existing bitmap must have been decoded from the same file format
The existing bitmap must have exactly the same width and height as the new image
The existing bitmap must have been `recycle()`d before being passed in
The existing bitmap must be mutable and its allocation big enough for the new decode
questions.explanation: Since API 19 the reused bitmap only needs to be mutable with an allocation byte count at least as large as the new image needs. The exact-size rule was the older pre-KitKat restriction, and a recycled bitmap cannot be reused because its pixels are gone.
